title: How does a naturally high and low fibre white bread affect digestion, blood sugar and appetite?
official: Determining the effect of high and low arabinoxylan breads on gut content along the entire gastrointestinal tract, metabolic responses and satiety regulation
summary:
Background and study aims 
The UK recommends that adults eat 30 g of fibre a day, but most people eat only about half that. Bread is a major source of fibre, yet most people choose white bread, which is low in fibre. The main fibre in white flour is called arabinoxylan. Rothamsted Research has developed wheat that is naturally higher in arabinoxylan, so white bread made from it looks and tastes like ordinary white bread but contains more fibre. This study aims to find out how eating this higher-fibre white bread for 2 weeks, compared with a lower-fibre white bread, affects digestion inside the gut, blood sugar, the gut hormones that control appetite, how full people feel and how much they eat.

Who can participate? 
Healthy men and women aged 18 to 65 years with a body mass index (BMI) of 18 to 30 kg/m². 

What does the study involve? 
Participants first attend a screening visit with a blood test, heart tracing (ECG), blood pressure, height and weight. They then complete two study periods, one with each bread, in a random order. Participants are not told which bread they are eating. The periods are separated by at least 4 weeks.

Each period starts with a 3–4 hour morning visit. A small tube (cannula) is placed in an arm vein, participants eat two slices of bread, and blood samples and appetite questionnaires are taken over 3 hours. Breath, urine and stool samples are collected, and participants are offered a pasta meal. Participants then eat 6 slices of the study bread a day at home for 2 weeks; the bread is delivered to them.

Each period ends with a 3-day (2-night) stay at the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility, Hammersmith Hospital. On Day 1, a thin, flexible tube is passed through the nose into the lower small intestine, guided by X-ray (fluoroscopy) at Charing Cross Hospital. On Day 2, a second tube is passed through the other nostril into the upper small intestine. On Days 2 and 3, participants eat set meals that include the study bread. Small samples of gut contents and blood are taken before and for up to 3 hours after meals, and participants complete appetite questionnaires and breath tests. Urine and a daily stool sample are collected. On Day 3, the tubes are removed and participants are offered a pasta meal so that the amount they eat can be measured. Participants also complete an online food diary (Intake24) on the day before each visit.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
There is no direct benefit to participants. Participants are reimbursed for their time and travel. The cannula may cause minor discomfort or bruising. The nasal tubes commonly cause temporary throat discomfort, a sore mouth, thirst, difficulty swallowing or hoarseness. Serious problems such as bleeding or damage to the gut are very rare. The X-ray procedures give a small radiation dose: about 1.62 mSv in total, similar to 9 months of natural background radiation in the UK. This adds about 0.008% to a person's lifetime risk of cancer. 

Where is the study run from? 
Imperial College London, at the NIHR Imperial Clinical Research Facility, Hammersmith Hospital (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
November 2026 to September 2028.

Who is funding the study? 
Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC) (UK).

Who is the main contact? 
Dr Begum Celik, bcelik@ic.ac.uk

interventions.name:
This is a randomised, single-blind, two-period crossover study. Participants are randomised to the order of the two breads using Sealed Envelope, by a researcher independent of the study. Participants are blinded to bread type. The two periods are separated by a washout of at least 4 weeks.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Male or female
2. Age between 18-65 years (inclusive)
3. Body mass index (BMI) of 18-30 kg/m2
4. Able to understand written and spoken English
5. Willingness and ability to give written informed consent and willingness and ability to understand, to participate and to comply with the study requirements
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Participants whose screening blood results are clinically significant
2.	Weight change of > = 5 kg in the preceding 2 months 
3.	Current smokers or individuals who vape
4.	Abnormal ECG
5.	History of substance abuse and/or excess alcohol intake 
6.	Pregnancy 
7.	breastfeeding 
8.	Diabetes 
9.	Cardiovascular disease
10.	Having polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
11.	Cancer 
12.	Gastrointestinal disease e.g. inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome 
13.	Kidney disease 
14.	Liver disease 
15.	Pancreatitis 
16.	Known food allergy or intolerance that would preclude consumption of the study breads or standardised meals, including coeliac disease and wheat or gluten sensitivity
17.	Started new medication within the last 3 months likely to interfere with energy metabolism, appetite regulation and hormonal balance, including: anti-inflammatory drugs or steroids, antibiotics, androgens, phenytoin, erythromycin or thyroid hormones
18.	Previous nasal fractures, or surgery, obstructed nasal airway, previous bowel surgery, previous abdominal trauma
19.	Any blood donation within the 12-week period prior to entering this study
20.	Subjects who are unable to give informed consent by themselves
21.	Subjects who are currently participating in other clinical trials

Any participants with the above conditions would already have an altered pattern of hormones and inflammatory molecules because of their disease process and would therefore give us confounding or misleading results.
